question: What if friction vanished for 5 seconds?
answer_in_one_line: Nothing can grip anything: feet cannot push, a cup slips through closed fingers, a leaning ladder slides flat, and because no lawn is level (building codes ask for 6 inches of fall in 10 feet so rain runs off) everything on it, heavy or light, slides downhill together: 20 feet in 5 seconds, ending at a jogging pace, pulled by just 9 pounds on a 180-pound man.

why_this_one: The trend file offers no fresh row that passes all four tests, so this is the best unused tier A entry of the topic bank, from a cluster that neither of the last two episodes used (the snail, the cloud). Everybody has slipped on ice or a wet floor and knows what one second without grip feels like; the question asks for five. The title is seven plain words. A 1,640-subscriber channel reached 2.7M views with it, so the topic pulls without a big channel behind it. The surprise is carried by one number anyone can check: a lawn that looks flat falls 6 inches in 10 feet, and with nothing to hold on to that is a 20-foot slide in 5 seconds, the same for a heavy pot, a man and a teacup. The mechanism (surfaces are bristles that lock) is carried by two brushes pressed together. It is drawable with the kit's garden and flat cards. The story stays in one back garden, away from roads and cars; Gus belly-flops onto his lawn inside his fishbowl and gets up beaming; nobody is hurt and there is nothing a child could copy.
